editor_spans.body: The full Motherwell speech partly answers the test set here last week, that the offer would be genuine only if it carried money and powers. The Prime Minister did not only urge Holyrood to devolve. He offered to hand over some of Westminster's own power: a devolved model of DWP employment support, plus innovation, enterprise and employability funding matched to Scottish regions. Offering away reserved powers is a different act from lecturing another government about centralisation.

The design still has a flaw. The employment model is to be 'shaped by Holyrood', so whether the Easterhouse principle of 'names not numbers' ever reaches an estate depends on Edinburgh passing power further down. That is the same Edinburgh the Prime Minister says is too slow on local government reform. He can open the door, but he cannot walk anyone through it.

The more telling detail is that the National Economic Council will meet the First Ministers for the first time since he took office. Britain's arrangements between its governments are still run by occasional summits and goodwill rather than standing institutions. A promise to work together that depends on one Prime Minister's temperament will last only as long as he is in office. If he means 'place-first', he should make the joint body permanent and give it a statutory footing.

The bus story is the most honest part of the speech. Buying Alexander Dennis vehicles meant paying 'even a little more' to sustain Scottish communities. That is a real break with the Treasury habit of buying the cheapest contract anywhere in the world, the same accounting under which Ravenscraig's closure looked rational from hundreds of miles away. If all UK procurement is to work that way, ministers should publish the premium they are willing to pay and change the value-for-money rules openly. Otherwise the old orthodoxy will quietly reassert itself.

The numbers he cited show how slow this work will be. Ravenscraig's site is still being filled more than thirty years on. One in six young people are not in education, employment or training. Life expectancy differs by seven years across ten miles. Deindustrialisation took a generation to do this, and devolution deals will take at least as long to undo it. Judge them on a decade of results, not one summit.
